In the late summer of 2022, the fine arts competition at the Colorado State Fair awarded first prize in its digital art category to an image that its creator had neither drawn, painted, nor photographed. The picture, a luminous tableau of robed figures gazing through a cavernous circular aperture, had been conjured with a text-to-image program called Midjourney. Its creator, a designer of tabletop games, had typed hundreds of painstaking prompts, culled one result from a welter of candidates, and burnished it with editing software before printing it on canvas. When he trumpeted his victory online, the backlash was swift and largely vitriolic. Some artists decried the win as chicanery; others lamented that years of apprenticeship could now be eclipsed by a few lines of text.
The judges later conceded that they had not grasped how the image had been produced, although the entry had been submitted under a name that included the program. The category had been defined capaciously, as artistic practice that used digital technology in the creative process, and nothing in its rules contemplated software that could generate a finished picture from a sentence. The imbroglio thus exposed less a lapse in one entrant's probity than a lacuna in the vocabulary of the institutions that judge art.
The following spring, the conundrum resurfaced in a more acute form. A German photographer won a category of a major international photography award with an eerie portrait of two women, then revealed that the image had been generated by software and declined the prize. He explained that he had entered as a test, to find out whether such competitions were prepared for machine-made work, and the answer, manifestly, was that they were not.
Legal institutions have been grappling with a cognate question: who, if anyone, owns such an image? The United States Copyright Office has repeatedly held that copyright protects only works of human authorship. When the Colorado prizewinner sought to register his picture, the office refused, reasoning that the portions engendered by the software could not be claimed by him, however assiduously he had honed his prompts. In 2025 a federal appeals court in Washington affirmed, in a separate case, that a work produced autonomously by a machine cannot be registered at all.
Competitions have since begun to recalibrate. Many now oblige entrants to disclose whether and how generative tools were used, and some have created separate categories for machine-assisted work, much as photography was once cordoned off from painting. Such rules are unlikely to adjudicate the deeper dispute about whether typing a prompt is closer to commissioning a picture or to composing one. They do, however, restore something the Colorado judges lacked: the information requisite to decide what, exactly, they are rewarding.

For more than two thousand years, many philosophers tacitly accepted an answer to one of the most venerable questions in their discipline: what is knowledge? The answer, often traced to a dialogue of Plato, holds that to know something is to have a belief that is true and that is buttressed by good reasons. A fortuitous guess is not knowledge, because it lacks justification; a scrupulously reasoned conviction that happens to be false is not knowledge either, because it lacks truth. Conjoin the three ingredients, the analysis claimed, and knowledge ensues.
In 1963 a then-obscure American philosopher named Edmund Gettier published a paper of barely three pages that upended this consensus. Gettier did not offer a new theory. He merely adduced cases in which a person holds a belief that is both justified and true, yet which hardly anyone would call knowledge. The anatomy of such cases is easy to replicate. Imagine a woman who glances at the clock in a railway station, sees that it reads twenty past two, and concludes that it is twenty past two. She has every reason to trust the clock, which has always been unfailingly accurate, and it is in fact twenty past two. Unbeknownst to her, however, the clock stopped exactly twelve hours earlier. Her belief is true, and it is justified, but its truth has nothing to do with her reasons. She has, in effect, been the beneficiary of a fluke.
The force of the example lies in how it sunders two things that ordinarily travel in tandem. Usually, the reasons that justify a belief are also what make it true, or at least what tether it to the truth. In cases of this kind the tether is severed: the justification points in one direction, the truth arrives from another, and the two converge only by happenstance.
Philosophers responded with prodigious energy. Some proposed appending a fourth condition, requiring that the belief not be inferred from any falsehood. Others argued that the belief must be caused in the right way by the fact it concerns, or that it must issue from a reliable process. Each proposal, however, soon met a fresh counterexample, often contrived by tweaking the details of its predecessor, and the literature burgeoned into an intricate contest between definitions and the puzzles devised to confound them.
Whatever the eventual verdict, a three-page paper managed to transmute a hoary definition into an abiding problem. Some philosophers have concluded from its history that knowledge cannot be decomposed into simpler parts at all and should instead be treated as a primitive notion in its own right. Others suspect that laypeople may not share philosophers' intuitions about such cases, and they have begun to test those intuitions with surveys conducted across languages and cultures. What those surveys have found merits closer scrutiny.

For much of the twentieth century, psychologists wrote as though the people who walked into their laboratories could serve as proxies for humanity as a whole. Textbooks confidently expounded how people perceive, reason, and make moral judgments, but the evidence behind these descriptions came overwhelmingly from a meager sliver of the species. A survey of leading psychology journals published in 2008 found that roughly ninety-six percent of the participants in the studies it examined came from Western industrialized countries, which together contain only about twelve percent of the world's population. Many were undergraduates taking introductory psychology courses, recruited because they were convenient and inexpensive.
In 2010 a team of researchers led by Joseph Henrich gave this problem a pithy and memorable name. They described the typical research participant as WEIRD: Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic. The acronym was more than a quip. Collating studies that had compared disparate populations, the authors argued that WEIRD people are not merely a sample of humanity but, on many measures, an unusual one, frequently lying at the outermost fringe of the human range rather than near its middle.
Some of the most striking evidence came from visual perception, a domain long assumed to be immutably fixed by biology. In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two lines of equal length look unequal because one terminates in arrowheads splayed outward and the other in arrowheads folded inward. Studies conducted in the 1960s across more than a dozen societies found that the potency of the illusion varied enormously. American undergraduates were among the most susceptible, while some foraging groups in southern Africa were scarcely beguiled at all. One proposed explanation is that people reared among rectilinear buildings learn to read angles as cues to depth, an interpretation that remains contested but that at least shows how experience might shape even basic perception.
Analogous contrasts have appeared in studies of fairness, cooperation, and reasoning. In economic games where one player proposes how to apportion a sum of money and another may accept or reject the offer, what counts as an acceptable split differs considerably from one society to another. Tendencies that Western studies had treated as universal features of the mind turned out, in several cases, to be parochial habits.
The critique has spurred reforms, though more sluggish ones than its authors hoped. Some journals now ask researchers to describe their samples more precisely and to eschew claims about all humans when they have studied only a few. International collaborations that run the same experiment in dozens of countries have proliferated. Skeptics of the WEIRD argument note that many findings do replicate across cultures, and that diverse samples are costly to assemble. Yet the central point is difficult to impugn: a science that aims to describe human nature cannot rest on the idiosyncrasies of a small and unrepresentative group, however convenient that group may be to recruit.

For as long as I have walked city streets, graffiti has been treated as a blight to be expunged. City governments earmark large sums each year to scour walls, and in many places painting on property without permission remains a crime. Yet some of the same cities now tout mural districts to tourists, and works by celebrated street artists are sometimes excised from walls, shipped across oceans, and sold at auction. This reversal has raised a question that would once have sounded preposterous: should street art be preserved, and if so, by whom?
The most dramatic legal answer came from New York. For two decades, a group of old factory buildings in Long Island City known as 5Pointz served as an open-air gallery where the owner permitted aerosol artists to paint, and the site drew pilgrims from around the world. In 2013 the owner, planning to build apartments, had the walls whitewashed overnight. Artists sued under a federal law that protects certain works of recognized stature from intentional destruction, and in 2018 a judge awarded them 6.75 million dollars in damages. An appeals court upheld the decision in 2020. [A] The ruling dumbfounded many property owners, who had assumed that paint on their own walls was theirs to remove.
Preservation, however, engenders dilemmas of its own. [B] Much street art is meant to be transient; it responds to a particular place and moment, and part of its meaning lies in its exposure to weather, to other painters, and to erasure. Removing a mural to protect it can denude it of the context that gave it significance, turning a public gesture into a private commodity. Some artists have vehemently denounced dealers who detached their works from walls without consent and offered them for sale. [C]
The tension resurfaced in the summer of 2024, when an anonymous British street artist revealed a series of animal images on walls and shutters across London, one new image each day. Within days, several had been stolen, defaced, or taken down for safekeeping by property owners or local authorities, so that crowds of devotees arriving to glimpse a piece sometimes found only a bare surface. [D] The episode demonstrated how fame can make a work more vulnerable rather than less, since the higher its market value, the greater the temptation to purloin it.
Cities experimenting with policies have arrived at no single panacea. Some photograph and catalog murals before buildings change hands; some designate legal walls where painting is permitted and nothing is guaranteed to last; a few negotiate agreements in which owners promise to notify artists before a wall is altered. What these approaches share is a recognition that the choice is not simply between keeping and destroying. I have come to think that documentation, consent, and a candid acquiescence in impermanence honor street art more faithfully than any attempt to embalm it in place.

For much of the past decade, the auction rooms of New York, London, and Hong Kong seemed impervious to ordinary economic gravity. Canvases by illustrious names fetched sums that made headlines around the world, and each spring season appeared to eclipse the last. In 2024 the mood soured. An annual report on the global art market, published by an art fair together with a Swiss bank, estimated that total sales of art and antiques fell by about twelve percent that year, to roughly 57.5 billion dollars, following a smaller decline in 2023. The slump was steepest at the very apex: works priced above ten million dollars, the trophies that had once epitomized the market's glamour, changed hands far less often.
Several explanations have been proffered. Higher interest rates made borrowing more expensive and raised the returns obtainable from safer investments, diminishing the allure of an asset that yields no dividends and costs money to insure and store. Political turbulence, including elections in many major economies and armed conflicts in Europe and the Middle East, encouraged wealthy collectors to bide their time. Sellers, for their part, were loath to consign their choicest pieces to a skittish market, fearing that a lackluster result would publicly depress the value of an artist's entire body of work. The dearth of masterpieces on offer then compounded the impression of decline.
Yet the picture was not uniformly dismal. According to the same report, the number of transactions actually rose slightly, as buyers gravitated toward works costing a few thousand dollars rather than a few million. Online sales, which had mushroomed during the pandemic, retained much of their audience, and younger collectors evinced particular interest in prints, design objects, and works by artists who had not yet graduated to the major salesrooms.
This divergence intimates that the slowdown was less a collapse of interest in art than a retrenchment at the speculative end of the market. When credit is cheap, paintings by a small group of celebrated artists can behave like financial instruments, acquired in the expectation that someone will pay more in a few years. When credit becomes dear, that expectation wanes, and prices that rested on it begin to look precarious. Works bought primarily for pleasure are less exposed to such vicissitudes, because their owners harbor little intention of selling them.
For auction houses, which earn fees on the value of what they sell, the shift has been grueling, and some have pared staff and shortened their calendars. For many artists beneath the uppermost tier, by contrast, a market less fixated on record prices may prove healthier. The open question for the ensuing years is whether the record-setting atmosphere of the previous decade will revive when interest rates abate, or whether 2024 marked the terminus of an anomalous period in which a handful of names monopolized most of the attention and most of the money.

For years I have selected fonts from a menu without a moment's deliberation, as though letters cost nothing to make, and so, I suspect, have millions of others. In fact, a polished typeface can take an adroit designer years to complete. Each glyph must be drawn in several weights, calibrated against every other glyph, spaced so that common pairs nestle comfortably together, and scrutinized at sizes ranging from a footnote to a billboard. Yet the legal protection given to this labor varies remarkably from one jurisdiction to another, and the variation betrays how uneasily letterforms sit within the categories of intellectual property.
In the United States, the shapes of letters themselves are generally not protected by copyright. Courts and the Copyright Office have long held that an alphabet is a utilitarian implement, and that granting a monopoly over the rudimentary forms of letters would stymie the very communication that copyright is meant to foster. A designer may seek a design patent for a typeface, but such patents are costly, slow, and rarely pursued. What American law does protect is the font software: the digital file encoding the instructions that tell a computer how to draw each character. Duplicating that file without permission can infringe copyright, even though redrawing the printed letters by hand and building a new file from scratch would generally not.
Other legal systems demarcate the line differently. Several European countries shield typeface designs through design law, and the United Kingdom treats typefaces as artistic works, albeit with a briefer term of protection once they are exploited commercially. In South Korea, font files have been treated as computer programs, and typeface designs can also be registered as designs. Consequently, a practice that is licit in one country may be actionable in another.
These distinctions carry tangible consequences for ordinary users, who seldom peruse the licenses attached to the fonts they install. A license might countenance printing a poster but proscribe embedding the font in an app, or allow personal use while forbidding commercial distribution. In Korea, the problem became notorious during the 2010s, when schools, small businesses, and local offices received letters demanding payment for fonts found on their computers, sometimes installed years earlier by a predecessor. Some of these claims were legitimate; others were predatory attempts to extort settlements from people who had no idea what a font license was.
The episode prompted a judicious response: public bodies and corporations began disseminating free fonts with clear licenses, allowing anyone to use them in documents, signs, and products. Designers still need income, of course, and free fonts cannot supplant the craft of commissioned type. But transparency, I would argue, benefits everyone. A legal regime that leaves ordinary users befuddled as to whether opening a document makes them liable serves neither the designers it claims to protect nor the public that letters are meant to serve.

Suppose a linguist arrives among a community whose language no outsider has ever recorded. There is no dictionary, no bilingual speaker, and no shared vocabulary of any kind. A rabbit scurries past, and one of the speakers points and says gavagai. The linguist jots down a provisional entry: gavagai means rabbit. The scene is the starting point of one of the most provocative arguments in twentieth-century philosophy, propounded by the American philosopher W. V. O. Quine in his 1960 book Word and Object.
Quine asked what, precisely, could warrant the linguist's entry. [A] The speaker might mean rabbit, but he might equally mean an undetached part of a rabbit, a momentary stage in the life of a rabbit, or the abstract quality of rabbithood. Whenever a rabbit is present, all of these are concomitantly present, so ostension alone cannot tell them apart. The linguist could ask further questions, of course, by pointing at a rabbit's ear or asking whether this is the same gavagai as before. But to interpret the answers, the linguist must already have translated words such as same and part, and those translations are beset by exactly the same uncertainty.
Quine inferred that translation is indeterminate: two translation manuals could each fit all the evidence of speakers' behavior while ascribing divergent meanings to their words. [B] He did not claim merely that translation is arduous or that our evidence is incomplete. His more audacious claim was that there may be no fact of the matter for the evidence to be incomplete about. If every discernible disposition of the speakers is consistent with both manuals, then, for Quine, there is nothing further, concealed in their minds, that makes one manual correct and the other mistaken.
The argument has disquieting implications that extend well beyond fieldwork. [C] If meaning is fixed only by behavior, the same indeterminacy applies at home, between speakers of a single language. When a neighbor utters the word rabbit, I presume she means what I mean, but my confidence rests on the frictionless flow of our conversations rather than on any unmediated access to her thoughts.
Many critics have demurred at these conclusions. Some argue that the alternative translations Quine proposed are so outlandish that no reasonable linguist would entertain them, and that simplicity offers a legitimate reason to prefer rabbit. [D] Developmental psychologists have added an empirical wrinkle: toddlers acquiring words appear to assume, without being taught, that a new label refers to a whole object rather than to its parts or qualities. Whether such findings answer Quine or merely describe the heuristics by which humans cope with his puzzle remains moot. What is no longer debatable is that the homely scene of a rabbit and a pointing finger has become one of philosophy's most enduring thought experiments.

Surveys are among the most ubiquitous tools in the social sciences, and among the most easily distorted. The difficulty is not merely that respondents forget or misconstrue questions. It is that people asked about their own conduct tend to present themselves flatteringly, overreporting what is esteemed and underreporting what is frowned upon. Researchers dub this tendency social desirability bias, and it can skew results in ways that are hard to detect from the answers alone.
Elections furnish a convenient test, because official records show who actually voted. When studies have compared what respondents said with those records, a persistent fraction of people who professed to have voted turned out not to have done so. Similar gaps appear for behavior that carries a stigma: people tend to understate how much alcohol they consume, how often they shirk exercise, or whether they have ever cheated on an examination. Because the distortion runs in a foreseeable direction, it cannot simply be averaged away by asking more people.
One ingenious family of stratagems, first proposed by the statistician Stanley Warner in 1965, is known as the randomized response technique. In one simple version, researchers who wish to ascertain how many students have plagiarized an assignment ask each respondent to flip a coin privately before answering. If the coin shows heads, the respondent answers the sensitive question truthfully; if it shows tails, the respondent simply says yes, regardless of the truth. The interviewer never learns how the coin landed, so no individual yes can be construed as a confession. Yet because the probability of tails is known, the researcher can subtract the expected number of automatic yeses and estimate the true rate across the whole group.
The method trades individual precision for collective candor. It necessitates larger samples, since the stochastic noise must be averaged out, and it works only if respondents comprehend and trust the procedure. Some studies have found that people still balk at saying yes even when the coin instructs them to, apparently fretful about how the answer might look. Researchers have therefore devised variations, such as replacing the coin with a second, anodyne question whose answer distribution is already known.
Other strategies approach the problem from different angles. Self-administered questionnaires, completed privately on a screen rather than spoken aloud to an interviewer, tend to elicit more forthright answers about sensitive topics. Deft wording can also help, for instance by acknowledging that many people have engaged in a behavior before asking whether the respondent has. None of these techniques eradicates the bias entirely. What they share is an insight that the designers of surveys ignore at their peril: people answer questions not only to inform the questioner but also to curate the impression they make, and an honest answer must first be rendered safe to give.

Few cultural vogues of recent years have proliferated as swiftly as the immersive exhibition. Visitors enter a dim, cavernous hall in which the walls, the floor, and sometimes the ceiling are covered with moving projections; music swells; imagery cascades across every surface; and the boundary between viewer and artwork seems to evaporate. Shows built around the paintings of Van Gogh toured dozens of cities in North America and Europe in the early 2020s, often selling out weeks beforehand. In Tokyo, the digital art collective teamLab reopened its Borderless museum in a new downtown complex in 2024, after the original site, which had lured millions of visitors, closed in 2022. In South Korea, a studio that became renowned for a colossal wave that seemed to crash inside an outdoor LED screen in Seoul has since erected a chain of kindred venues.
It is worth distinguishing between two kinds of work that share the label. The first takes existing paintings, usually by venerated artists long deceased, and animates them: sunflowers undulate, stars swirl, and brushstrokes magnified to the size of a door drift past. The second consists of works conceived from the outset for projection and interaction, in which flowers bloom where visitors stand and digital waterfalls part around their bodies. The first is essentially a novel mode of presenting reproductions; the second is a new medium in its own right.
Critics have been acerbic about the first kind. Inflating a canvas to fill a warehouse, they argue, destroys precisely what makes it worth seeing: its scale, its texture, the vestiges of a hand at work on a surface of a particular size. A painting that once rewarded slow, intimate scrutiny degenerates into a backdrop for selfies, and the visitor's attention migrates from the work to the self within the work. To such critics, these spectacles resemble amusement parks more than galleries.
Defenders reply that many visitors to immersive shows have never entered an art museum and might never do so. If an animated sunflower impels even a fraction of them to seek out the original canvas, the facsimile has served art rather than betrayed it. They also point out that novel formats have perennially been disputed: color reproductions in books, too, were once impugned for cheapening the paintings they made widely available.
The second kind of work poses distinct conundrums. Because it exists only as software, light, and the movements of an audience, it cannot be bought, hung, or stored in the way a canvas can, and its survival hinges on equipment destined for obsolescence. Museums that wish to acquire it must adjudicate what, exactly, they are preserving: the code, the hardware, the experience, or detailed documentation of how the work once behaved. These are not trifling problems, and the way institutions answer them will shape which of today's immersive works can still be seen in fifty years.

In 1960 the physicist Eugene Wigner published an essay whose title has become a philosophical byword: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences. Wigner's puzzle was simple to state and stubbornly hard to dissolve. Mathematicians often develop ideas for reasons that have nothing to do with the physical world, guided by a sense of elegance, generality, or sheer inquisitiveness. Yet time and again, structures devised in this manner turn out, sometimes decades or centuries later, to describe nature with uncanny exactitude. Why should that be?
The exemplars are arresting. Complex numbers, which involve the square root of negative one, were long regarded with misgiving; the very epithet imaginary was affixed to them partly as a term of disparagement. Centuries later, they became indispensable to quantum mechanics, whose basic equations cannot be written without them. Non-Euclidean geometries, explored in the nineteenth century as rigorous alternatives to Euclid's assumption about parallel lines, seemed at first to be idle exercises devoid of application. Einstein's general theory of relativity then harnessed a curved geometry of this general kind to describe gravitation itself.
Several answers have been proposed. One, often associated with mathematical Platonism, posits that mathematical objects subsist independently of human minds and that the physical world is in some sense undergirded by them; mathematicians and physicists are therefore exploring the same reality from different directions. A second answer is more circumspect. Mathematics, it suggests, originally sprang from counting, measuring, and discerning regularities in the world, so it is scarcely surprising that its abstractions remain moored to the world, however far they seem to stray.
A third response queries whether the effectiveness is really as remarkable as Wigner claimed. Mathematicians generate a prodigious variety of structures, and physicists, when they need a tool, rummage among them for one that fits. We recall the triumphs and overlook the vast quantity of mathematics that has never described anything physical. On this view, the semblance of a miracle is partly an artifact of selection, akin to being astonished that a ring holding thousands of keys contains one that opens a particular door.
There is also the question of how effective mathematics really is outside physics. In biology, economics, and psychology, mathematical models are valuable but seldom attain the precision of physical laws, and some researchers suspect that the systems these sciences study are too labyrinthine to be captured by elegant equations. If so, Wigner's puzzle may illuminate as much about the peculiar simplicity of the physical problems that mathematics has solved as about mathematics itself. Whether that simplicity is a deep feature of the universe, or merely an echo of the questions physicists have chosen to ask, is the issue to which we must now turn.

Suppose a professor is asked to write a letter recommending a student for a teaching post in philosophy, and the letter says only that the candidate writes excellent English and has attended tutorials regularly. Nothing in the letter is false, and nothing in it is overtly disparaging. Yet any reader will surmise that the professor thinks poorly of the candidate's philosophical ability. The example comes from the British philosopher Paul Grice, whose lectures in the late 1960s furnished an influential account of how speakers communicate more than their words literally say.
Grice posited that conversation is governed by a tacit expectation of cooperation. Interlocutors assume that each contribution is designed to serve the shared purpose of the exchange, and Grice parsed this assumption into several maxims: be as informative as required, but not more; say only what you believe to be true; be relevant; and be clear, brief, and orderly. These maxims are [A] rules that speakers consciously consult; most people could not even name them. They codify what listeners take for granted when they try to make sense of what they hear.
The intriguing cases arise when a speaker appears to flout a maxim openly. The recommendation letter is glaringly less informative than the situation demands. Because the reader assumes the professor is still cooperating, the reader casts about for a rationale, and the most plausible one is that the professor has nothing favorable to say about the candidate's philosophy but is reluctant to commit it to paper. Grice christened such inferred meanings implicatures. They go [B] beyond what is literally said, yet they are dependably understood.
Implicatures elucidate a great many quotidian exchanges. If one friend asks whether another enjoyed a concert and receives the reply that the hall had very comfortable seats, the questioner gathers that the music disappointed. If a manager asks whether some of the reports are finished and is told that some are, she will usually infer that not all of them are, even though the word some is logically compatible with all.
A pivotal feature of implicatures is that they can be revoked without contradiction. The speaker who says that some of the reports are finished can [C] add that in fact all of them are, without retracting anything. By contrast, a speaker who says that all the reports are finished cannot then add that some are unfinished. This test has given linguists a serviceable tool for distinguishing what a sentence means from what a speaker merely suggests by uttering it.
Grice's framework has been amplified, criticized, and revised by subsequent theorists, some of whom argue that a single principle of relevance can subsume the work of all his maxims. Its central insight, however, has [D] proved durable: understanding a sentence is not simply a matter of decoding words, but of reasoning about why a rational, cooperative interlocutor would choose to say exactly that.

When an old building stands in the way of a new plan, the reflexive response in the city where I grew up, as in many others, has been to raze it. Demolition clears the site, eliminates the cost of repairing dilapidated structures, and allows designers to begin with a tabula rasa. Lately, however, a burgeoning cohort of architects and planners has begun to interrogate this habit, contending that the greenest building is often the one that already exists.
The argument rests partly on climate arithmetic. Buildings and construction together account for a large share of global carbon dioxide emissions, commonly reckoned at close to two-fifths when both the operation of buildings and the manufacture of their materials are included. Much attention has been lavished on making new buildings efficient to heat and cool. But producing cement and steel and hauling them to a site emits large amounts of carbon before a structure is ever occupied, and tearing down a sound building squanders the carbon already spent on it. A new, highly efficient building may need decades of lower energy bills to recoup the emissions caused by its own construction.
The case for reuse is not solely ecological. Old buildings carry memories, textures, and proportions that new ones struggle to emulate, and their conversion can conserve the character of a neighborhood while reinvigorating it. London's Tate Modern occupies a former power station on the bank of the Thames. In Seoul, an elevated roadway built in 1970 next to the main railway station was metamorphosed into a pedestrian garden in 2017, and the old station building itself has become a cultural venue. In 2021 the Pritzker Prize, often hailed as architecture's highest accolade, went to two French architects renowned for transforming run-down public housing blocks rather than replacing them, adding light, space, and winter gardens while tenants went on living there.
Reuse has its limitations, however. Some edifices are structurally unsound, contaminated, or so poorly insulated that retrofitting them would cost more, financially and environmentally, than starting again. Building codes drafted for new construction can make conversions onerous, and developers often find it simpler to forecast the profits of a new tower than the uncertainties of an old warehouse whose latent flaws surface only once work begins. Nor is every old building worth keeping; a city that preserved everything would leave no room for the exigencies of new generations.
The more fruitful question, as I see it, is not whether to preserve or to demolish in general, but how to decide in each case. Some municipalities now compel developers to estimate the carbon cost of demolition before permits are granted, and some proffer incentives for conversions. Such policies do not forbid new buildings. They simply ensure that the value locked up in existing ones, gauged in carbon as well as in memory, is reckoned before it is discarded.
